title: Warrant
pitch: Your agent can act on people it cannot name. The analyst who runs the report writes the tool it calls — a tool that was in nobody's source code, and that the page decides what may leave.
about_excerpt: Your agent can act on people it cannot name. The analyst who runs the report writes the tool it calls — a tool that was in nobody's source code, and that the page decides what may leave. Like Comment Story Updates Every number with the command that produced it: 0 identifiers returned, against 1,552 with the policy layer deleted. Taught with one month, asked for another. It follows the page's calendar instead of freezing on the month she demonstrated. "Who is emp_03u6yn?" No tool on this page returns it. Not discouraged: there is no code path. What an agent sees: 8 = 7 + 1. Seven the author wrote, one she made, read from getTools() rather than the page's own notes. Why each literal should vary, in the agent's own words, beside the schema the page generated. She can disagree with either. The workbench this team already uses. 1,680 rows, eight controls, and the seven tools its author wrote. An acting tool never acts alone. The call suspends, naming what it will do to how many people, until she confirms. A real agent's proposal, before the tool exists. OpenAI's Codex read the page's structure; the page validated what came back. The work done once, by hand. The log records what each operation meant, not where she clicked. Six months on, somebody reclassifies a field. They never heard of her tool and are changing something else. Its fingerprint no longer matches, so it leaves getTools() — gone from the list, not refused when called — until re-approved. Approval calls registerTool(). The tool exists now and declares the three fields it will never return. Eight edge cases generated from the page's own declaration and already run against real rows, before the tool exists. One control turns the proposal into a tool that acts, not only answers, with an edge case for how many people one call reaches. The person who runs the report writes the agent's tool. The same five rows twice: names on her screen, handles in what a tool returns. Inspiration Every tool an agent can call on the web was written by a developer, months earlier, in a schema fixed before anyone knew which question would be asked. That is the ceiling on the agentic web, and it is not a performance ceiling: the number of things an agent can do on a page is capped by how much a product team could anticipate. The obvious way through it — let the model do whatever it likes on the page — gives up the one thing the page is for. The page is where the rules live: which field is an identifier, who may see it, what a write costs. Warrant is the other way through. The person who does the work mints the tool. The page keeps the veto. She is an HR operations coordinator. On the first of every month she opens the same payroll screen, sets one period and one overtime cut-off, and reads off the eighteen people over the line. Three years, and nobody ever shipped her a button for it. Ask an agent instead and the answer comes back as eighteen real names and two national identifiers, in a chat log that syncs to somebody else's laptop — the page had a policy about those fields and the answer left without it. So: she demonstrates the report once . The page turns it into a typed tool any agent can call — name, parameters, defaults, limits, none of which were in anybody's source code. And the page, not the model, decides what that tool may return. A field marked pii is not discouraged from appearing in a result; there is no code path that puts it there. Six months later somebody reclassifies a field and the tool takes itself off the surface, whether or not anyone remembers it exists. What it is, in one session Live at warrant-gray.vercel.app , in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , or ChatGPT's in-app browser. No account, no backend. The workbench. Eight controls, 1,680 rows , seven tools its author wrote. The surface on the right is read from document.modelContext.getTools() , not the page's own bookkeeping. An agent drives her screen. run_query sets the controls in front of her and the table follows. Then it asks to group people by name and the screen refuses in place: POLICY_VIOLATION · employee_name is pii and cannot be returned as a group key. She demonstrates. Month 2026-08 , overtime above 40 . Two operations recorded — what they meant, not where she clicked. Her agent proposes the tool through propose_tool , saying which literals should vary. The page validates it against its own field declaration; a parameter it does not permit comes back No field named month . Eight edge cases run against the real rows before the tool exists — the month rolling over, a period with no data, a withheld field asked for by name. Approval stays disabled until every one is judged by a person. Approve. registerTool() runs. The surface reads 8 = 7 + 1 . Ask it for a month nobody demonstrated: "the one before" resolves to 2026-07 . Ask who emp_03u6yn is — no tool returns it. Ask to flag them and the call suspends inside the page until she decides; decline and the agent gets declined_by_human , nothing written. Reclassify a field. The fingerprint no longer matches and the tool leaves getTools() — gone from the list, not refused when called — until a person re-approves it. The whole argument, in five numbers Entries in this challenge describing runtime tool creation, counted generously 116 of 868 …in which a non-developer doing their own job decides the tool's shape 3 Identifiers reaching a tool result, against 1552 with the policy layer deleted 0 An agent never told the tool exists reaches for it on the question it was made for 21 of 24 Assertions behind that, offline and against the deployed site 80 + 21 + 13 + 10 The first two say what is new here. Not runtime tool creation — between 19 (a narrow pattern), 62 (an outside reading) and 116 (widened until it hurts) other entries describe that, and webmcp-evaluator/field_position.py ships with all 868 pages so you can re-run the count and watch it get worse for us. What stays rare is who decides the shape . All 116 were read one at a time, without knowing which row was this project: in the great majority a developer decides the shape in code or config, and the rest divide between a model writing it, an imported OpenAPI or marketplace document, and a shape compiled out of the page's own DOM. In 3 the person doing their own job decides it. That number was 1 in an earlier draft and it was wrong; a reader found Understudy , the selecting regex could not see it, and widening the net surfaced XACT FOUNDRY as well. Both are named, with the argument against our own claim, in webmcp-evaluator/authorship.md . How far it goes The tail this reaches cannot be shipped by hand, and here that is arithmetic rather than rhetoric. The eight controls on one workbench express 1,572,480 distinct questions — 13 × 7 × 4 × 4 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 5, every factor a dropdown you can count. A generic query tool reaches all of them, and this page ships one, so the gap is not expressiveness. It is that none of those questions
video_transcript_excerpt: This is Warrant, built on WebMCP. The person who runs the report writes the tool, and the page still decides what it may return. Somebody runs the same report on the first of every month, and has for years. Nobody shipped a button for it. It is this period, that cut-off, minus the exceptions the team knows. So, they ask an agent instead, and the answer comes back with 18 real names and two national identifiers in it. Warrant is an ordinary internal screen whose tool surface is not fixed at build time. A person does the work once. Approval turns it into a tool. The claim is worth one number. Take the policy layer out, and the same questions return 1552 with it, zero. Here is the product it happens in. The same five rows, twice. Her screen names them. What the tool returns does not. An ordinary payroll workbench, and the seven tools its author wrote. None answers her question, so she does it once by hand. First, what the tool called does here. It is not a data API beside the page. Run query sets the controls on her own screen. The filters move, and the table follows. Then it asks to group people by name, and the screen turns it down in front of her. National ID is restricted. There is no code path that returns it. It reads the page's structure through the browser's tool list, groups by department, and answers. Then ask it for the names. It returns handles instead. And it names the three fields the page would tell, because the page told it so. The agent proposes a tool, and the page checks it against its own declaration. It says why each literal should vary. Month repeats, so a demonstrated one goes stale. The page runs eight Dutch cases against real rows before the tool exists. She judges each one. She approves. WebMCP's registered tool runs, and the browser's own tool list goes from seven to 8. It was taught with 1 month. Ask it for a month nobody demonstrated. Ask it who one of these people is. No tool on this page returns it. It can still act on them. Add note does not return. It suspends in psych a page while she decides. She declines and the agent is told of human declined. That is the part with no server side equivalent. There is nobody at a server to ask. The 108 agent runs across two model families. Have told to get an eight aug. Zero names. None of this is written for people ops. Three sites share one implementation. The same code runs a support desk and an emergency department. Later, the page changes. Someone reclassifies the department field. The tool's fingerprint no longer matches, so it is unregistered. Gone from get tools. Not refused when called. A tool nobody wrote in the source that everybody had a hand in and echo page can still say no to.

live_observation.first_impression: A polished landing page explains a Warrant workbench for minting policy-scoped agent tools and offers an Open the workbench link.
live_observation.action_attempted: Opened the workbench and inspected the People ops dataset and available controls.
live_observation.after_state: The workbench displayed filters, a large employee table with redacted sensitive fields, tool-surface controls, and a Reveal identifiers button.
live_observation.notes: The page visibly supports the claimed workbench flow; no identifiers were revealed.
